overview: Diplodocus carnegii ("Carnegie's double beam") was one of the longest animals ever to walk the Earth, reaching 26 metres, though far lighter than the stocky Brachiosaurus at around 15 tonnes. Its neck was held roughly horizontally rather than upright, and the peg-like teeth at the very front of the snout were used exclusively for raking leaves from branches — Diplodocus could not chew and processed no food in the mouth at all.

Andrew Carnegie funded plaster casts of the famous specimen "Dippy" that were shipped to eight museums across Europe, making Diplodocus the most publicly recognised sauropod of the 20th century. The NHM London's Dippy stood in the main entrance hall for 112 years before being replaced by the blue whale skeleton Hope in 2017.

articles.title: Carnegie and the plaster Dippies
articles.body: Andrew Carnegie funded expeditions that recovered the CM 84 specimen from Wyoming in 1899. After seeing a newspaper illustration, Carnegie commissioned eight full-scale plaster casts for European royalty — gifts to the natural history museums of London, Paris, Berlin, Vienna, Bologna, La Plata, Saint Petersburg and Madrid. This act of scientific philanthropy made Diplodocus the most-recognised dinosaur skeleton in the world for much of the 20th century.

articles.title: Feeding mechanism
articles.body: The pencil-like peg teeth of Diplodocus are positioned only at the front of the snout and show heavy wear on their tips — consistent with raking leaves off branches. No shearing or grinding occurs in the mouth; food was swallowed whole and processed by gastroliths (stomach stones) and fermentation. This feeding strategy allowed Diplodocus to strip enormous volumes of vegetation rapidly, an efficient if crude approach for a 15-tonne browser.

articles.title: Neck posture debate
articles.body: Computer modelling of Diplodocus neck vertebrae and joint mobility consistently suggests the neck was held near-horizontal or at a slight upward angle — very different from the giraffe-like posture of early reconstructions. At maximum horizontal extension the neck allowed feeding across a wide swathe of ground-level vegetation without moving the body, an efficient strategy for a very large animal whose locomotion was energetically costly.

record.description: Diplodocus was a long-necked diplodocid sauropod from the Morrison Formation of western North America. D. carnegii and related material provide several substantial skeletons and skulls, but famous museum mounts are composites and species assignments have been extensively revised.
facts: The Carnegie mount combines principal specimens and reconstructed parts; it is not one complete individual.
Peg-like front teeth and low skull support selective cropping, while exact vegetation and feeding height varied with posture.
Extreme tail-whip speeds and supersonic cracking remain biomechanical hypotheses rather than consensus facts.

presentation.heroLead: The archetypal long-necked, whip-tailed sauropod, known from several substantial skeletons whose casts, sent around the world by Andrew Carnegie, made it one of the first dinosaurs to become globally famous.

heroMedia.title: Life restoration of Diplodocus carnegii
heroMedia.alt: Life restoration of the sauropod Diplodocus carnegii in side view, with a long horizontal neck and whip-like tail
heroMedia.caption: Life restoration by Fred Wierum. Proportions follow the Carnegie Museum skeletons; the row of small spines along the back is based on a skin impression from an unidentified diplodocid, and colour is interpretive.

animalParagraphs: Diplodocus was a very long but comparatively lightly built sauropod of the Late Jurassic Morrison Formation. Diplodocus carnegii, the best-known species, reached about twenty-four to twenty-six metres from snout to tail tip, most of that length made up of a long neck and an even longer tail. Mass estimates of roughly twelve to fifteen tonnes are model-dependent.

The skull was long and low with nostrils set high on the head and slender, pencil-like teeth confined to the front of the jaws. Tooth wear shows that the animal cropped or stripped vegetation rather than chewing it. The forelimbs were shorter than the hindlimbs, giving the back a gentle slope, and the tail ended in a run of thin, rod-like vertebrae often described as a whip.

Diplodocus is the name-bearing genus of Diplodocidae, but its own taxonomy is untidy. The original type species, D. longus, rests on tail bones that most recent workers consider undiagnostic, and a 2015 specimen-level revision proposed D. carnegii as the new type species. The giant D. hallorum, once named Seismosaurus, is now generally included in the genus.
animalHighlights: A long, low skull with nostrils high on the head and slender peg-like teeth at the front of the jaws.
An extremely long tail of more than eighty vertebrae, tapering to a thin, whip-like tip.
Forelimbs shorter than hindlimbs, with a single large claw on each hand.

lifeCards.label: Feeding
lifeCards.level: Supported by skull and tooth wear
lifeCards.reason: Peg-like teeth with wear facets and rapid tooth replacement indicate cropping or branch-stripping. Feeding height depends on neck posture models rather than direct evidence.

lifeCards.label: Movement
lifeCards.reason: Complete limbs and girdles from several skeletons and Morrison sauropod trackways establish four-legged walking. Rearing on the hindlimbs is a hypothesis.

lifeCards.label: Known size
lifeCards.reason: Two associated Carnegie skeletons fix the length of D. carnegii closely. D. hallorum was larger, perhaps over thirty metres, but is less complete, and all masses depend on the method used.

lifeCards.label: Appearance
lifeCards.reason: Proportions are secure. Skin impressions from Morrison diplodocids show small scales and a row of keratinous spines, but none is certainly Diplodocus, and colour is unknown.

whereFacts.label: Type locality
whereFacts.value: Garden Park, Fremont County, Colorado, USA (D. longus); Sheep Creek, Albany County, Wyoming, USA (D. carnegii)

locality.name: Sheep Creek
locality.note: Morrison Formation. The D. carnegii holotype was excavated here in 1899; the original D. longus type came from Garden Park near Cañon City, Colorado.

presentation.classificationSummary: Diplodocus gives its name to Diplodocidae and Diplodocinae within Diplodocoidea. Its position is stable; the open issues are which species are valid, whether D. longus can remain the type species, and how many historic specimens truly belong to the genus.

related.reason: Compare with the heavier-built apatosaurine that lived alongside it.
Compare with a close diplodocine relative with a longer neck and shorter tail.
Compare with a giant Morrison diplodocid known from far less complete material.

questions.title: Which species is the type?
questions.copy: D. longus was named first, on tail vertebrae that are hard to diagnose. A petition proposed D. carnegii as the type species instead; until that is settled, the genus name rests on shaky foundations.

questions.title: How did it hold its neck?
questions.copy: Reconstructions range from a near-horizontal neck to a raised one. Joint anatomy, cartilage and soft tissue all affect the answer, and no posture is directly recorded.

questions.title: Could the tail crack like a whip?
questions.copy: Computer models have suggested the tail tip could move very fast, but claims of supersonic cracking remain untested hypotheses rather than accepted fact.

review.ageReviewNote: Most diagnostic Diplodocus material comes from Kimmeridgian-Tithonian Morrison intervals near 154-152 Ma.

specimens.name: Holotype of Diplodocus longus
specimens.note: Tail vertebrae and chevrons from Garden Park, Colorado, named by Marsh in 1878. Widely regarded as undiagnostic at species level.

specimens.name: Holotype of Diplodocus carnegii
specimens.note: A largely complete postcranial skeleton from Sheep Creek, Wyoming, described by Hatcher in 1901 and the core of the Carnegie mount and its many casts. CM 94 is the associated paratype skeleton.

specimens.name: Holotype of Diplodocus hallorum
specimens.institution: New Mexico Museum of Natural History and Science
specimens.note: Partial skeleton from New Mexico originally named Seismosaurus; one of the largest diplodocids known.

panel.headline: Several substantial skeletons, but famous mounts are composites and the type species is in doubt.
panel.standfirst: Diplodocus is well sampled for a sauropod, with two associated Carnegie skeletons providing most of the postcranial skeleton and further partial skeletons from Colorado, Wyoming, Utah and New Mexico. Skulls are known but their species-level referral is debated, and the original type material is a set of tail bones.

coverage.label: Excellent
coverage.basis: Every skeletal region is represented across multiple individuals; the neck-to-tail series is nearly complete in the Carnegie specimens, although no single individual is complete with its skull.

knownRemains.title: What is actually preserved?
knownRemains.summary: Nearly complete vertebral columns including the long whip tail, pectoral and pelvic girdles, complete fore- and hindlimbs, ribs and chevrons, plus several skulls with braincases and teeth from Morrison quarries. The Carnegie holotype and paratype together supply most of the skeleton.
knownRemains.note: The celebrated Carnegie mount and its casts combine CM 84 with CM 94 and other specimens, with a skull and feet modelled from other animals. Diplodocus skulls are known, but which species they belong to is contested.

materialGroups.label: Skull and jaws
materialGroups.value: Several long, low skulls with braincases and pencil-like teeth from Morrison quarries; species referral of most is debated.

materialGroups.label: Vertebral column
materialGroups.value: Near-complete cervical, dorsal, sacral and caudal series including the whip-like tail tip, with ribs and the double-beamed chevrons that give the genus its name.

materialGroups.label: Girdles and limbs
materialGroups.value: Complete shoulder and hip girdles, forelimbs and hindlimbs with hands and feet from several individuals.

materialGroups.label: Exceptional preservation
materialGroups.value: Skin impressions with small scales and keratinous spines are known from Morrison diplodocids but not securely from Diplodocus; no colour or gut contents are known.

specimenCards.title: YPM 1920 · holotype of D. longus
specimenCards.description: Tail vertebrae and chevrons collected at Garden Park, Colorado, and named by Marsh in 1878. Most recent workers consider them undiagnostic, which is why D. carnegii has been proposed as a replacement type species.

specimenCards.title: CM 84 · holotype of D. carnegii
specimenCards.description: A largely complete postcranial skeleton excavated at Sheep Creek, Wyoming, in 1899 and described by Hatcher in 1901. With the paratype CM 94 it formed the basis of the Carnegie mount and the casts sent to museums worldwide.
specimenCards.meta: Sheep Creek, Wyoming · Morrison Formation · Carnegie Museum of Natural History

interpretation.label: Directly observed
interpretation.value: Several partial to near-complete postcranial skeletons, multiple skulls, isolated bones and Morrison sauropod trackways.

interpretation.label: Scientific interpretation
interpretation.value: A lightly built, low- to mid-browsing diplodocine that cropped or stripped vegetation with its peg-like teeth and used its tail for balance and perhaps defence or display.

interpretation.label: Still unknown
interpretation.value: The valid species list, the identity of the type species, habitual neck posture, real tail performance, precise mass and all colour and most soft tissues.
